Listener perception of disfluent robot voice: Statistical report

Xinyi

2026-05-10

This document presents the data analysis from a study investigating how Mandarin Chinese listeners perceive disfluency in robot speech. The study examined whether hesitations (e.g., “um” and “uh”) enhance listeners’ memory retention and how they influence subjective ratings such as naturalness, friendliness, and vividness.

Experiment 1 explored the effects of voice type (pre-recorded vs. synthetic), story fluency (fluent vs. with filled pauses), and interaction type (baseline vs. robot-interaction).

Experiment 2 adopted a within-subjects design using only natural voice stimuli with increased recall difficulty. These experiments tested the effect of story fluency across three conditions: fluent, filled pause, and silent pause.

The report includes: A data overview, Analysis of Experiment 1, Analysis of Experiment 2

1 Load Organized Data

1.1 Variable definitions

  • Variables in the trials dataset (trials):

    • PARTICIPANTID = unique participant identifier
    • Experiment = experiment the participant took part in
    • InteractionType = whether the participant interacted with a robot
    • VoiceType = voice type condition of the experiment
    • StoryFluency = fluency condition of the story
    • StoryID = story identifier
    • PlotID = plot identifier within each story
    • QUESTION_ID = unique code combining StoryID and PlotID
    • TaskType = type of task completed by the participant
    • PlotType = whether the plot could include a disfluency (“uh” or “um”); Critical if yes, control if no
    • ANSWER = participant’s transcribed and coded answer
    • IsAnswerCorrect = binary indicator of answer correctness for analysis

  • Variables in the participant dataset (participants):

    • PARTICIPANTID = unique participant identifier
    • Experiment = experiment the participant took part in
    • InteractionType = whether the participant interacted with a robot
    • VoiceType = voice type condition of the experiment
    • Story1Fluency = fluency condition of story 1
    • Story2Fluency = fluency condition of story 2
    • Story3Fluency = fluency condition of story 3
    • NATURALNESS_RATING = naturalness rating provided by the participant
    • FRIENDLINESS_RATING = friendliness rating provided by the participant
    • VIVIDNESS_RATING = vividness rating provided by the participant
    • Age = participant age in years
    • Gender = participant gender(Female, Male)

  • Variables in the stimuli dataset (stimuli):

    • StoryID = story identifier
    • PlotID = plot identifier within each story
    • QUESTION_ID = unique code combining StoryID and PlotID
    • PlotType = whether the plot could include a disfluency (“uh” or “um”); Critical if yes, control if no
    • PlotText= plot text in Chinese Mandarin
    • PlotText_EN= plot text translated to English
    • TaskinExp1= the task type in Experiment 1
    • TaskinExp2= the task type in Experiment 2
trials <- read.csv("../data/trials.csv", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
participants <- read.csv("../data/participants.csv", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)
stimuli <- read.csv("../data/stimuli.csv", stringsAsFactors = TRUE)


# Relevel StoryFluency factor - set "Fluent" as reference level
trials$StoryFluency <- factor(trials$StoryFluency, levels = c("Fluent", "FilledPause", "SilentPause"))

participants$Story1Fluency <- factor(participants$Story1Fluency, levels = c("Fluent", "FilledPause", "SilentPause"))
participants$Story2Fluency <- factor(participants$Story2Fluency, levels = c("Fluent", "FilledPause", "SilentPause"))
participants$Story3Fluency <- factor(participants$Story3Fluency, levels = c("Fluent", "FilledPause", "SilentPause"))

2.2 exp1 Naturalness Ratings

Plotting average naturalness rating score by VoiceType and StoryFluency

# Extract naturalness ratings for exp1
naturalness_exp1 <- participants %>%
  filter(Experiment == "exp1") %>%
  filter(!is.na(NATURALNESS_RATING)) %>%
  select(PARTICIPANTID, VoiceType, Story1Fluency, NATURALNESS_RATING, InteractionType) 

cat("Experiment 1 naturalness ratings:", nrow(naturalness_exp1), "observations\n")
## Experiment 1 naturalness ratings: 129 observations
# Summary statistics
naturalness_exp1_summary <- naturalness_exp1 %>%
  group_by(VoiceType, Story1Fluency, InteractionType) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_rating = mean(NATURALNESS_RATING, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd_rating = sd(NATURALNESS_RATING, na.rm = TRUE),
    se_rating = sd_rating / sqrt(n),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

2.2.1 Statistical model for naturalness in Experiment 1

# make sure the variables are converted to factors 
naturalness_exp1$VoiceType <- factor(naturalness_exp1$VoiceType, levels = c("Pre-recorded", "Synthetic"))
naturalness_exp1$StoryFluency <- factor(naturalness_exp1$StoryFluency, levels = c("Fluent", "FilledPause"))
naturalness_exp1$InteractionType <- factor(naturalness_exp1$InteractionType, levels = c("Baseline", "Robot-interaction"))

# apply contrasted coding 

contrasts(naturalness_exp1$VoiceType) <- contr.sum(2) / 2
contrasts(naturalness_exp1$StoryFluency) <- contr.sum(2) / 2
contrasts(naturalness_exp1$InteractionType) <- contr.sum(2) / 2

contrasts(naturalness_exp1$VoiceType) 
##              [,1]
## Pre-recorded  0.5
## Synthetic    -0.5
contrasts(naturalness_exp1$StoryFluency)
##             [,1]
## Fluent       0.5
## FilledPause -0.5
contrasts(naturalness_exp1$InteractionType) 
##                   [,1]
## Baseline           0.5
## Robot-interaction -0.5
# Ordinal regression models
# Full model
natural_model_exp1_full <- clm(factor(NATURALNESS_RATING) ~ VoiceType * StoryFluency * InteractionType, 
                           data = naturalness_exp1)
summary(natural_model_exp1_full)
## formula: 
## factor(NATURALNESS_RATING) ~ VoiceType * StoryFluency * InteractionType
## data:    naturalness_exp1
## 
##  link  threshold nobs logLik  AIC    niter max.grad cond.H 
##  logit flexible  129  -190.29 404.59 6(0)  5.45e-14 1.4e+02
## 
## Coefficients:
##                                            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
## VoiceType1                                 1.254348   0.341561   3.672  0.00024
## StoryFluency1                              0.830578   0.330586   2.512  0.01199
## InteractionType1                          -0.007095   0.324743  -0.022  0.98257
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1                   0.227219   0.652044   0.348  0.72749
## VoiceType1:InteractionType1                0.869170   0.651800   1.333  0.18237
## StoryFluency1:InteractionType1             0.185978   0.649238   0.286  0.77453
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1:InteractionType1  2.227416   1.308564   1.702  0.08872
##                                              
## VoiceType1                                ***
## StoryFluency1                             *  
## InteractionType1                             
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1                     
## VoiceType1:InteractionType1                  
## StoryFluency1:InteractionType1               
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1:InteractionType1 .  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Threshold coefficients:
##     Estimate Std. Error z value
## 2|3  -3.1293     0.4009  -7.806
## 3|4  -1.7159     0.2439  -7.034
## 4|5  -1.0747     0.2093  -5.134
## 5|6   0.7512     0.2012   3.734
## 6|7   2.7587     0.3507   7.867

A cumulative link model revealed a significant main effect of voice type, with pre-recorded voices rated as more natural than synthetic voices (β = 1.25, z = 3.67, p < .001). Story fluency also showed a significant main effect, with fluent stories rated as more natural than stories containing filled pauses (β = 0.83, z = 2.51, p = .012). These effects were qualified by a marginal three-way interaction between voice type, story fluency, and interaction type (β = 2.23, z = 1.70, p = .089).

2.2.2 emmeans comparison for naturalness rating in Experiment 1

# use emmeans on the latent scale
# For cumulative logit models: A difference on the latent scale is already a log–odds ratio.

emm_voice <- emmeans(natural_model_exp1_full,
                   ~ VoiceType | StoryFluency * InteractionType,
                   mode = "latent")
pairs(emm_voice)
## StoryFluency = Fluent, InteractionType = Baseline:
##  contrast                   estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  (Pre-recorded) - Synthetic    2.359 0.729 Inf   3.236  0.0012
## 
## StoryFluency = FilledPause, InteractionType = Baseline:
##  contrast                   estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  (Pre-recorded) - Synthetic    1.018 0.665 Inf   1.532  0.1256
## 
## StoryFluency = Fluent, InteractionType = Robot-interaction:
##  contrast                   estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  (Pre-recorded) - Synthetic    0.377 0.640 Inf   0.588  0.5564
## 
## StoryFluency = FilledPause, InteractionType = Robot-interaction:
##  contrast                   estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  (Pre-recorded) - Synthetic    1.263 0.601 Inf   2.101  0.0357
## 
## Note: contrasts are still on the factor scale. Consider using
##       regrid() if you want contrasts of back-transformed estimates.
emm_fluency <- emmeans(natural_model_exp1_full,
                   ~ StoryFluency | VoiceType * InteractionType,
                   mode = "latent")
pairs(emm_fluency)
## VoiceType = Pre-recorded, InteractionType = Baseline:
##  contrast             estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  Fluent - FilledPause    1.594 0.692 Inf   2.304  0.0212
## 
## VoiceType = Synthetic, InteractionType = Baseline:
##  contrast             estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  Fluent - FilledPause    0.253 0.683 Inf   0.370  0.7110
## 
## VoiceType = Pre-recorded, InteractionType = Robot-interaction:
##  contrast             estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  Fluent - FilledPause    0.294 0.619 Inf   0.476  0.6344
## 
## VoiceType = Synthetic, InteractionType = Robot-interaction:
##  contrast             estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  Fluent - FilledPause    1.181 0.619 Inf   1.906  0.0566
## 
## Note: contrasts are still on the factor scale. Consider using
##       regrid() if you want contrasts of back-transformed estimates.

Because interactions were included in the model, main effects reflect average tendencies across conditions, and follow-up analyses were conducted to clarify condition-specific differences.

Follow-up comparisons using estimated marginal means on the latent scale showed that pre-recorded voices were rated as significantly more natural than synthetic voices in the Fluent–Baseline condition (β = 2.36, z = 3.24, p = .001) and in the FilledPause–Robot condition (β = 1.26, z = 2.10, p = .036). No reliable differences were observed in the remaining conditions.

Similarly, fluent stories were rated as significantly more natural than disfluent stories in the Pre-recorded–Baseline condition (β = 1.59, z = 3.24, p = .021). No reliable differences were observed in the remaining conditions.

While mean friendliness ratings appeared broadly similar across conditions, ordinal regression revealed a small but significant effect of interaction type. Participants were more likely to give higher friendliness ratings in the robot interaction condition than in the baseline condition (β = −0.69, SE = 0.33, z = −2.08, p = .038). No other main effects or interactions were significant.

  )

2.4.2 Statistical model for vividness in Experiment 1

# make sure the variables are converted to factors 
vividness_exp1$VoiceType <- factor(vividness_exp1$VoiceType, levels = c("Pre-recorded", "Synthetic"))
vividness_exp1$StoryFluency <- factor(vividness_exp1$StoryFluency, levels = c("Fluent", "FilledPause"))
vividness_exp1$InteractionType <- factor(vividness_exp1$InteractionType, levels = c("Baseline", "Robot-interaction"))

# apply contrasted coding 

contrasts(vividness_exp1$VoiceType) <- contr.sum(2) / 2
contrasts(vividness_exp1$StoryFluency) <- contr.sum(2) / 2
contrasts(vividness_exp1$InteractionType) <- contr.sum(2) / 2

contrasts(vividness_exp1$VoiceType) 
##              [,1]
## Pre-recorded  0.5
## Synthetic    -0.5
contrasts(vividness_exp1$StoryFluency)
##             [,1]
## Fluent       0.5
## FilledPause -0.5
contrasts(vividness_exp1$InteractionType) 
##                   [,1]
## Baseline           0.5
## Robot-interaction -0.5
# Ordinal regression
vividness_model_exp1_full <- clm(factor(VIVIDNESS_RATING) ~ VoiceType * StoryFluency * InteractionType, 
                        data = vividness_exp1)
summary(vividness_model_exp1_full)
## formula: factor(VIVIDNESS_RATING) ~ VoiceType * StoryFluency * InteractionType
## data:    vividness_exp1
## 
##  link  threshold nobs logLik  AIC    niter max.grad cond.H 
##  logit flexible  122  -189.40 404.81 5(0)  7.05e-07 9.9e+01
## 
## Coefficients:
##                                           Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
## VoiceType1                                  0.7810     0.3368   2.319   0.0204
## StoryFluency1                               0.1893     0.3309   0.572   0.5673
## InteractionType1                            0.2836     0.3312   0.856   0.3919
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1                   -0.2416     0.6608  -0.366   0.7147
## VoiceType1:InteractionType1                 1.3967     0.6725   2.077   0.0378
## StoryFluency1:InteractionType1             -0.5949     0.6626  -0.898   0.3693
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1:InteractionType1   0.7435     1.3236   0.562   0.5743
##                                            
## VoiceType1                                *
## StoryFluency1                              
## InteractionType1                           
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1                   
## VoiceType1:InteractionType1               *
## StoryFluency1:InteractionType1             
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1:InteractionType1  
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Threshold coefficients:
##     Estimate Std. Error z value
## 1|2  -3.8428     0.5894  -6.520
## 2|3  -2.9558     0.3963  -7.459
## 3|4  -1.9578     0.2703  -7.243
## 4|5  -0.5445     0.1946  -2.798
## 5|6   1.0682     0.2133   5.007
## 6|7   3.0859     0.4259   7.246

A cumulative link model revealed a significant main effect of voice type on vividness ratings, with pre-recorded voices rated as more vivid than synthetic voices (β = 0.78, z = 2.32, p = .020). This effect was moderated by interaction type, as indicated by a significant Voice Type × Interaction Type interaction (β = 1.40, z = 2.08, p = .038).

The voice-type advantage for pre-recorded voices is larger in the Baseline condition than in the Robot-interaction condition.

emm_vivid <- emmeans(
  vividness_model_exp1_full,
  ~ VoiceType | InteractionType,
  mode = "latent"
)
## NOTE: Results may be misleading due to involvement in interactions
pairs(emm_vivid)
## InteractionType = Baseline:
##  contrast                   estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  (Pre-recorded) - Synthetic   1.4794 0.495 Inf   2.990  0.0028
## 
## InteractionType = Robot-interaction:
##  contrast                   estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  (Pre-recorded) - Synthetic   0.0827 0.456 Inf   0.181  0.8562
## 
## Results are averaged over the levels of: StoryFluency 
## Note: contrasts are still on the factor scale. Consider using
##       regrid() if you want contrasts of back-transformed estimates.

Follow-up comparisons on the latent scale showed that pre-recorded voices were rated as significantly more vivid than synthetic voices in the Baseline condition (β = 1.48, z = 2.99, p = .003), whereas no difference was observed in the Robot-interaction condition (β = 0.08, z = 0.18, p = .86).

The advantage of pre-recorded voices in perceived vividness appears only in the baseline interaction condition and disappears in the robot interaction condition.

2.6 Multiple-choice (stories 1&2) statistical modeling in exp1

2.6.1 Statistical analysis for multiple-choice questions

# All mixed-effects models included random intercepts for participants and items (question ID) to account for variability in overall response accuracy across individuals and questions.

model_mcq_exp1_full <- glmer(IsAnswerCorrect ~  VoiceType * StoryFluency * InteractionType + (1|PARTICIPANTID) + (1 | QUESTION_ID), data = story12_exp1, family = "binomial",
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))
)
summary(model_mcq_exp1_full)
## Generalized linear mixed model fit by maximum likelihood (Laplace
##   Approximation) [glmerMod]
##  Family: binomial  ( logit )
## Formula: IsAnswerCorrect ~ VoiceType * StoryFluency * InteractionType +  
##     (1 | PARTICIPANTID) + (1 | QUESTION_ID)
##    Data: story12_exp1
## Control: glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e+05))
## 
##      AIC      BIC   logLik deviance df.resid 
##    559.6    602.2   -269.8    539.6      514 
## 
## Scaled residuals: 
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -4.6315 -0.6582  0.3909  0.5640  1.2381 
## 
## Random effects:
##  Groups        Name        Variance Std.Dev.
##  PARTICIPANTID (Intercept) 0.3399   0.5830  
##  QUESTION_ID   (Intercept) 0.6312   0.7945  
## Number of obs: 524, groups:  PARTICIPANTID, 131; QUESTION_ID, 4
## 
## Fixed effects:
##                                           Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)
## (Intercept)                                 1.3544     0.4221   3.209  0.00133
## VoiceType1                                  0.1347     0.2462   0.547  0.58432
## StoryFluency1                               0.5481     0.2475   2.215  0.02677
## InteractionType1                            0.2152     0.2462   0.874  0.38214
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1                   -0.2547     0.4926  -0.517  0.60505
## VoiceType1:InteractionType1                 1.5712     0.4982   3.154  0.00161
## StoryFluency1:InteractionType1              0.2869     0.4923   0.583  0.56006
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1:InteractionType1  -0.0871     0.9844  -0.088  0.92949
##                                             
## (Intercept)                               **
## VoiceType1                                  
## StoryFluency1                             * 
## InteractionType1                            
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1                    
## VoiceType1:InteractionType1               **
## StoryFluency1:InteractionType1              
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1:InteractionType1   
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Correlation of Fixed Effects:
##             (Intr) VcTyp1 StryF1 IntrT1 VcT1:SF1 VT1:IT SF1:IT
## VoiceType1   0.015                                            
## StoryFlncy1  0.045 -0.004                                     
## IntrctnTyp1  0.044  0.133  0.030                              
## VcTyp1:StF1 -0.008  0.095  0.032  0.040                       
## VcTyp1:InT1  0.064  0.134  0.057  0.041  0.021                
## StryFl1:IT1  0.012  0.042  0.133  0.097  0.131   -0.003       
## VT1:SF1:IT1  0.011  0.027  0.131 -0.007  0.131    0.094  0.036

A generalized linear mixed-effects model revealed a significant main effect of story fluency on answer accuracy, with higher accuracy for fluent stories than for stories containing filled pauses (β = 0.55, z = 2.22, p = .027). This effect was qualified by a significant interaction between voice type and interaction type (β = 1.57, z = 3.15, p = .002), indicating that the influence of voice type on answer accuracy depended on the interaction context.

2.6.2 Post-hoc analysis for multiple-choice questions model in exp1

emm_mcq <- emmeans(model_mcq_exp1_full, ~ VoiceType | InteractionType, type = "link")
## NOTE: Results may be misleading due to involvement in interactions
pairs(emm_mcq)
## InteractionType = Baseline:
##  contrast                   estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  (Pre-recorded) - Synthetic    0.920 0.373 Inf   2.468  0.0136
## 
## InteractionType = Robot-interaction:
##  contrast                   estimate    SE  df z.ratio p.value
##  (Pre-recorded) - Synthetic   -0.651 0.326 Inf  -1.997  0.0459
## 
## Results are averaged over the levels of: StoryFluency 
## Results are given on the log odds ratio (not the response) scale.

Follow-up comparisons on the logit scale showed that, in the Baseline condition, answers were significantly more likely to be correct when participants heard pre-recorded voices than synthetic voices (β = 0.92, z = 2.47, p = .014). In contrast, in the Robot-interaction condition, answers were significantly more likely to be correct when participants heard synthetic voices than pre-recorded voices (β = −0.65, z = −2.00, p = .046).

synthetic voice may have disproportionately influence the memory performance

2.8 Statistical modeling for retelling task in exp1

For retelling accuracy, mixed-effects models included random intercepts for participants and questions to account for individual differences and item difficulty; no random slopes were included because predictors were not fully crossed within participants or items.

model_retelling_exp1_fourway <- glmer(IsAnswerCorrect ~  VoiceType * StoryFluency * InteractionType * PlotType + (1|PARTICIPANTID) + (1 | QUESTION_ID), data = story3_exp1, family = "binomial",
  control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 2e5))
)

## InteractionType1:PlotType1                          -0.06478    0.22062  -0.294

## StoryFluency1:InteractionType1:PlotType1            -0.18096    0.44095  -0.410
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1:InteractionType1:PlotType1  0.48145    0.88232   0.546
##                                                     Pr(>|z|)  
## (Intercept)                                           0.6870  
## VoiceType1                                            0.1034  
## StoryFluency1                                         0.2609  
## InteractionType1                                      0.0854 .
## PlotType1                                             0.1230  
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1                              0.3554  
## VoiceType1:InteractionType1                           0.5990  
## StoryFluency1:InteractionType1                        0.3913  
## VoiceType1:PlotType1                                  0.4815  
## StoryFluency1:PlotType1                               0.6909  
## InteractionType1:PlotType1                            0.7690  
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1:InteractionType1             0.1011  
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1:PlotType1                    0.7925  
## VoiceType1:InteractionType1:PlotType1                 0.1434  
## StoryFluency1:InteractionType1:PlotType1              0.6815  
## VoiceType1:StoryFluency1:InteractionType1:PlotType1   0.5853

## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Correlation matrix not shown by default, as p = 16 > 12.
## Use print(x, correlation=TRUE)  or
##     vcov(x)        if you need it

A generalized linear mixed-effects model of retelling accuracy, including random intercepts for participants and questions, revealed no reliable main effects of voice type, story fluency, or interaction type, and no significant interactions among these factors. Although there was a marginal three-way interaction between voice type, story fluency, and interaction type (β = 1.24, z = 1.72, p = .086), this effect did not reach conventional significance and was not further decomposed. Overall, retelling accuracy was dominated by participant- and item-level variability rather than experimental manipulations.

While voice type and interaction context influenced subjective experience and multiple-choice comprehension, these effects did not extend to retelling accuracy once item difficulty was accounted for.

Interim discussion: Across subjective ratings and memory accuracy, filled pauses showed no memory benefit and sometimes worsened outcomes.

Fluent speech consistently improved naturalness ratings and multiple-choice accuracy, while effects on friendliness, vividness, and retelling were weak or inconsistent. Overall, the effects of disfluencies were measure- and context-dependent, with stronger impacts on structured comprehension than on social evaluation or generative recall.

Experiments 2 focus on retelling tasks only, where genuine disfluency effects were observed with pre-recorded voice, and extend to silent pauses to test whether hesitation benefits generalize across disfluency types.

3 Analysis 3: Experiments 2

Experiment 2

  • Each participant experiences all 3 stories (S1, S2, S3) - within-subjects
  • Each story has different StoryFluency for each participant
  • 6 counterbalanced conditions distribute fluency levels across stories

# Extract ratings data - each participant should have one rating per interaction type
# Since ratings are given for the overall experience, we take the first non-NA rating per participant
ratings_exp2 <- participants %>%
  filter(Experiment == "exp2") %>%
  filter(!is.na(NATURALNESS_RATING) | !is.na(FRIENDLINESS_RATING) | !is.na(VIVIDNESS_RATING)) %>%
  group_by(PARTICIPANTID, InteractionType) %>%
  summarise(
    # Take first non-NA rating (they should all be the same for a participant anyway)
    NATURALNESS_RATING = first(NATURALNESS_RATING[!is.na(NATURALNESS_RATING)]),
    FRIENDLINESS_RATING = first(FRIENDLINESS_RATING[!is.na(FRIENDLINESS_RATING)]),
    VIVIDNESS_RATING = first(VIVIDNESS_RATING[!is.na(VIVIDNESS_RATING)]),
    Story1Fluency = Story1Fluency,
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  # Remove rows where all ratings are NA
  filter(!is.na(NATURALNESS_RATING) | !is.na(FRIENDLINESS_RATING) | !is.na(VIVIDNESS_RATING))

3.2 Experiment 2 Ratings Visualization

Plotting average naturalness rating score, friendliness score and vividness score by interaction type

# Define rating variables and labels
rating_vars_clean <- c("NATURALNESS_RATING", "FRIENDLINESS_RATING", "VIVIDNESS_RATING")
rating_labels <- c("Naturalness", "Friendliness", "Vividness")

plots_list <- list()

# Ensure factor order consistency
ratings_exp2$InteractionType <- factor(ratings_exp2$InteractionType,
                                       levels = c("Baseline", "Robot-interaction"))

# Loop through rating variables
for (i in 1:length(rating_vars_clean)) {
  rating_var <- rating_vars_clean[i]
  rating_label <- rating_labels[i]
  
  plot_data <- ratings_exp2 %>%
    filter(!is.na(.data[[rating_var]]))
  
  if (nrow(plot_data) > 0) {
    
    # Summary statistics (optional print)
    summary_stats <- plot_data %>%
      group_by(InteractionType) %>%
      summarise(
        n = n(),
        mean_rating = mean(.data[[rating_var]], na.rm = TRUE),
        sd_rating = sd(.data[[rating_var]], na.rm = TRUE),
        se_rating = sd_rating / sqrt(n),
        .groups = "drop"
      )
    
    cat(paste0("\n", rating_label, " summary:\n"))
    print(summary_stats)
    
    # Visualization (aligned with 1a style)
    p <- ggplot(
      plot_data,
      aes(x = InteractionType, 
          y = .data[[rating_var]],
          fill = InteractionType,
          pattern = InteractionType)
    ) +
      stat_summary(
        fun = "mean",
        geom = "bar_pattern",
        position = position_dodge(0.9),
        colour = "black",
        pattern_fill = "black"
      ) +
      stat_summary(
        fun.data = mean_se,
        geom = "errorbar",
        width = 0.08,
        position = position_dodge(0.9)
      ) +
      scale_fill_manual(
        name = "Interaction Type",
        values = wes_palette(n = 3, name = "Chevalier1")
      ) +
      scale_pattern_manual(
        name = "Interaction Type",
        values = c("none", "stripe")  # Baseline = none, Robot-interaction = stripe
      ) +
      guides(
        fill = guide_legend(
          override.aes = list(
            pattern = c("none", "stripe"),
            pattern_fill = c("black", "black"),
            pattern_density = c(0, 0.3)
          )
        ),
        pattern = "none"
      ) +
      labs(
        x = "Interaction Type",
        y = paste(rating_label, "Rating"),
        title = paste(rating_label, "Ratings in Experiments 2")
      ) +
      coord_cartesian(ylim = c(1, 7)) +
      scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
      theme_classic() +
      theme(
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.title = element_text(size = 12),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 11),
        strip.text = element_text(size = 11),
        legend.position = "bottom"
      )
    
    plots_list[[rating_label]] <- p
  }
}

3.5 Statistical modeling for Experiment 2 memory results

Sum coded analysis for experiment 2

Story fluency was manipulated at the passage level, whereas plot type (critical vs control plot points) was an item-level characteristic. Because only critical plot points were preceded by interruptions, the interaction between story fluency and plot type tests whether disfluency has a local effect on the interrupted plot points or a global effect on discourse encoding that also influences control plot points. Interaction type (baseline vs Robot-interaction) was included to test whether these effects differ by interaction context.

contrasts(trials_exp2$StoryFluency)   <- contr.sum(3) /2
contrasts(trials_exp2$PlotType)     <- contr.sum(2) /2
contrasts(trials_exp2$InteractionType) <- contr.sum(2) /2  

contrasts(trials_exp2$StoryFluency)

## Fluent       0.5  0.0
## FilledPause  0.0  0.5
## SilentPause -0.5 -0.5
contrasts(trials_exp2$PlotType)
##          [,1]
## Control   0.5
## Critical -0.5
contrasts(trials_exp2$InteractionType)

## Baseline           0.5
## Robot-interaction -0.5

m0 <- glmer(IsAnswerCorrect ~InteractionType * PlotType * StoryFluency  +
              (1|PARTICIPANTID) + (1|QUESTION_ID),
            data=trials_exp2, family=binomial,
            control = glmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa"))

A generalized linear mixed-effects model of retelling accuracy, including random intercepts for participants and questions, revealed a significant main effect of story fluency. Specifically, fluent stories were recalled more accurately than the average of filled-pause and silent-pause stories (β = 0.19, z = 2.28, p = .023). In contrast, filled-pause stories tended to show reduced accuracy relative to the average of fluent and silent-pause stories, although this effect was marginal (β = −0.16, z = −1.95, p = .052). No reliable main effects of interaction type or plot type were observed, and no significant interactions emerged, indicating that the effect of story fluency on retelling accuracy was largely consistent across interaction contexts and plot types.

3.5.1 Post-Hoc test for the modeling result

## NOTE: Results may be misleading due to involvement in interactions
pairs(emm_fluency)

##  Fluent - SilentPause        0.1104 0.0731 Inf   1.511  0.2858

Follow-up comparisons using estimated marginal means showed that fluency effects were present in Critical plots but not in Control plots: in Critical plots, fluent stories were recalled more accurately than both filled-pause (β = 0.25, SE = 0.13, p = .049) and silent-pause stories (β = 0.25, SE = 0.13, p = .042), whereas no differences between fluency conditions were observed in Control plots (all ps ≥ .26). All other two-way and three-way interactions were not significant.

Although allowing participant-specific slopes for story fluency significantly improved model fit, the pattern of fixed effects was unchanged; therefore, results are reported from the simpler random-intercept model for clarity.
